Synthetic long-form lesson marker. This lesson exists only to exercise the reading layout: it is long enough to need contents, and it carries every kind of technical block the renderer supports.

## Why batching changes the economics

A model server that handles one request at a time leaves most of the accelerator idle. Batching groups requests so one pass over the weights serves many of them, which is how a fixed hardware budget turns into more completed requests. The first idea to hold on to is that the weights are read once per pass, however many requests ride along. A reader who already knows [the failure modes](ref:knowledge.catalog-e2e-sections) of a cache can skim the next paragraph.

Memory traffic, not arithmetic, usually sets the pace. Each decode step reads every weight to produce a single token for each request in the batch, so the cost of a step barely grows as the batch grows, until the batch becomes large enough that arithmetic starts to matter. That crossover is where throughput stops improving and latency starts to suffer.

::: callout kind=note
Everything in this lesson is synthetic and invented for layout testing. The numbers are placeholders, not measurements of any real system.
:::

### The latency budget

Interactive use sets a latency budget before any batching decision is made. If a reader expects the first token within a fraction of a second and subsequent tokens at reading speed, then the scheduler may only wait so long to fill a batch. The longer it waits, the larger the batch, and the later the first request in that batch gets its answer.

Two numbers describe the budget. The queueing delay is how long a request waits before it joins a batch. The step time is how long one pass takes once it has. The sum of the first and a handful of the second is what a user feels.

### Throughput versus tail latency

Raising the batch size raises throughput and, past some point, raises the slowest requests' latency faster than the average. Tail latency is what breaks a service level objective, so tuning for the average hides the problem. The table below compares three synthetic operating points; the identifiers are deliberately long so the table is wider than a phone.

| `synthetic_operating_point` | `synthetic_batch_size_limit` | `synthetic_p50_latency_ms` | `synthetic_p99_latency_ms` | `synthetic_tokens_per_second` | `synthetic_cost_per_million_tokens` |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| `value_conservative_operating_point` | `value_batch_size_limit_8` | `value_p50_latency_ms_120` | `value_p99_latency_ms_210` | `value_tokens_per_second_900` | `value_cost_per_million_tokens_high` |
| `value_balanced_operating_point` | `value_batch_size_limit_32` | `value_p50_latency_ms_180` | `value_p99_latency_ms_420` | `value_tokens_per_second_2600` | `value_cost_per_million_tokens_medium` |
| `value_aggressive_operating_point` | `value_batch_size_limit_128` | `value_p50_latency_ms_340` | `value_p99_latency_ms_1500` | `value_tokens_per_second_4100` | `value_cost_per_million_tokens_low` |

Read down a column to see the trade. Read across a row to see what one setting costs elsewhere.

## Sizing the `kv_cache` budget

Each request in flight keeps a cache of the keys and values it has produced so far, so that a new token does not recompute the whole history. The cache grows with every token, and it lives in the same scarce memory as the weights. How many requests fit in a batch is therefore decided by memory long before arithmetic.

::: callout kind=tip
Budget the cache for the longest context you intend to serve, then check how many such requests fit. A scheduler that admits more than that will evict, and eviction is a latency spike nobody planned for.
:::

### A back-of-the-envelope estimate

Work the estimate per token first, then multiply. The per-token cost is two tensors, for keys and for values, across every layer, at the numeric width in use. Multiply by the context length for one request, then by the batch size for the whole batch.

```python
def synthetic_kv_cache_bytes(layers, kv_heads, head_dim, dtype_bytes, context_tokens, batch_size):
    per_token = 2 * layers * kv_heads * head_dim * dtype_bytes  # keys and values for every layer
    return per_token * context_tokens * batch_size


def synthetic_max_batch_for_budget(budget_bytes, layers, kv_heads, head_dim, dtype_bytes, context_tokens):
    one_request = synthetic_kv_cache_bytes(layers, kv_heads, head_dim, dtype_bytes, context_tokens, batch_size=1)
    return int(budget_bytes // one_request)


class SyntheticAdmissionController:
    def __init__(self, budget_bytes, layers, kv_heads, head_dim, dtype_bytes, max_context_tokens, reserve_fraction=0.1):
        self.budget_bytes = int(budget_bytes * (1.0 - reserve_fraction))
        self.limit = synthetic_max_batch_for_budget(self.budget_bytes, layers, kv_heads, head_dim, dtype_bytes, max_context_tokens)
        self.running = 0

    def try_admit(self, request_id, prompt_tokens, requested_new_tokens):
        if self.running >= self.limit:
            return {"admitted": False, "reason": "kv_cache_budget_exhausted", "request_id": request_id, "retry_after_ms": 50}
        self.running += 1
        return {"admitted": True, "request_id": request_id, "prompt_tokens": prompt_tokens, "reserved_new_tokens": requested_new_tokens}

    def release(self, request_id):
        self.running = max(0, self.running - 1)
        return {"released": request_id, "running": self.running}
```

The estimate ignores paging overhead and fragmentation, which is why a real system reserves a margin. The reserve fraction above is that margin.

### Example

Take a deployment with a fixed cache budget and a target context length. Divide the budget by the cost of one request at that length. The result is the number of requests that can be in flight at once, and it is a ceiling, not a target.

## Where the pipeline spends its time

Before a request reaches the accelerator it passes through several stages, and each can become the bottleneck. A diagram of the shortest useful path makes the ordering concrete.

```mermaid
graph LR
  Client[Client] --> Gateway[Gateway] --> Server[Model server]
```

Real deployments add stages, and the diagram grows with them. The next diagram shows a fuller path with long stage names, and it is wider than any column of text, so it must scroll instead of shrinking until the labels cannot be read.

```mermaid
graph LR
  A[Client request arrives at the edge gateway] --> B[Admission control and quota check]
  B --> C[Prompt tokenization and prefix cache lookup]
  C --> D[Scheduler assigns a continuous batch slot]
  D --> E[Prefill on the prompt processing pool]
  E --> F[Decode on the token generation pool]
  F --> G[Streaming response assembly and filtering]
  G --> H[Usage metering and audit logging]
```

### Prefill and decode

Prefill processes the whole prompt at once and is limited by arithmetic. Decode produces one token at a time and is limited by memory traffic. Serving them on the same accelerator makes them interfere, which is why some systems split them across pools and ship the cache between them. Whether that split pays for itself depends on how long the prompts are and how much the transfer costs. A reader comparing designs can practise exactly this reasoning on [a design problem](ref:problem.p2-t4-practice), and the [earlier lesson](ref:lesson.catalog-e2e-second) covers the arithmetic.

::: callout kind=warning
Do not tune the batch size on average latency alone. A change that improves the average can quietly push the slowest requests past the objective.
:::

### Example

A second worked case, kept short so the duplicate heading above gets its own anchor. Suppose prompts are long and answers are short. Prefill dominates, the decode pool idles, and splitting the two pools raises utilisation. Suppose instead that prompts are short and answers are long. Decode dominates and the split buys little.

## Why [batching](ref:knowledge.t24-premium-deep-dive) is not the whole story

Batching is one lever among several. Quantisation shrinks the weights and the cache, which raises the batch limit directly. Speculative decoding spends spare arithmetic to produce several tokens per pass. Prefix caching avoids recomputing a shared prompt. Each interacts with the others, and each moves the point where the trade-offs bite.

### Putting it together

Choose the latency budget first, because it is a requirement, then the cache budget, because it is a constraint, and only then the batch size, because it is a consequence. Reversing that order is the most common way to build a system that benchmarks well and serves badly.

#### A short checklist

- State the latency objective for the first token and for later tokens.
- Compute the cache cost of one request at the longest supported context.
- Divide the memory budget by that cost and keep a reserve.
- Measure tail latency, not only the average, at the chosen limit.

## Summary

Batching trades latency for throughput, memory decides how far that trade can go, and the order in which you fix the budgets decides whether the result is a service or a benchmark. The practice problems that follow ask you to make exactly these choices.

items.title: Attention
items.summary: How a model weighs which parts of its input matter for each output.

sections.title: Definition
sections.text: Attention is a way for a model to decide, for the position it is producing, how much to draw on every other position in its input. The result is a weighted blend of the input, where the weights are learned from data rather than fixed in advance.

sections.title: Why it matters
sections.text: A fixed-size summary loses detail on long inputs. Attention lets the model look back at the part of the input that matters for the step it is on, which is why it sits underneath most modern language and retrieval systems.

sections.title: How it works
sections.text:
Each position produces three vectors: a **query**, a **key** and a **value**. A query is compared with every key to give a score, the scores are normalised into weights, and the output is the weighted sum of the values.

| Step | Operation | Shape per head |
|---|---|---|
| Score | query · key | sequence × sequence |
| Normalise | softmax over keys | sequence × sequence |
| Blend | weights × values | sequence × head_dim |

```python
def synthetic_attention(query, key, value):
    scores = query @ key.T / (key.shape[-1] ** 0.5)
    weights = softmax(scores, axis=-1)
    return weights @ value
```

The score matrix is why cost grows with the square of the sequence length.

sections.title: Building blocks
sections.text:
Three learned projections feed one scoring step. Several of these run side by side as heads, and their outputs are concatenated and projected once more.

```mermaid
graph LR
  Input --> Projections[Query, key and value projections] --> Scores --> Weights --> Output
```

sections.title: When to use
sections.text: Reach for attention when the output at one position depends on a few input-dependent positions elsewhere: translation, summarisation, re-ranking retrieved passages.

sections.title: When not to use
sections.text: Be cautious when sequences are so long that comparing every pair is the constraint, or when a fixed local window already captures the dependency.

sections.title: Trade-offs
sections.text:
- Expressive: any position can influence any other.
- Costly: time and memory grow with the square of the length.
- Flexible: the same block serves text, images and audio.

sections.title: Where it goes wrong
sections.text: Attention weights are tempting to read as an explanation, but they show where the model looked, not why it answered as it did. Long inputs can also dilute the weights until nothing stands out.

sections.title: Worked example
sections.text: Take a three-token input. The query for the last token scores highest against the key of the first token, so most of the output is that token's value. Change the input and the same query attends elsewhere.

sections.title: Example: masking
sections.text: When generating text, each position may attend only to earlier ones. A mask sets the scores for later positions to negative infinity before the softmax, so their weights become zero.

sections.title: In an interview
sections.text: Be ready to state the quadratic cost and name one way to reduce it. Expect a follow-up on why the scores are scaled before the softmax.

items.title: Batching
items.summary: Group requests so one pass over the model serves many of them.

sections.title: Definition
sections.text: Batching holds requests briefly and runs them through the model together, so the cost of reading the weights is shared.

sections.title: When to use
sections.text: Use it when requests arrive faster than one accelerator can serve them one at a time and a little added waiting is acceptable.

sections.title: Trade-offs
sections.text: Larger batches raise throughput and raise the latency of the slowest request. The waiting time you allow is the dial between them.

sections.title: Failure modes
sections.text: A batch that waits for a slow request holds up every other request in it. Cap the wait, not only the size.

items.title: Embedding
items.summary: A list of numbers that stands for the meaning of a piece of content.

sections.title: Definition
sections.text: An embedding maps a word, passage or image to a point in a space where nearby points have similar meaning.

sections.title: Why it matters
sections.text: Once content is a point, finding similar content is a distance calculation, which is what makes semantic search practical.

items.title: Evaluation metrics
items.summary: The numbers that say whether a model is doing its job.

sections.title: Definition
sections.text: An evaluation metric turns a model's outputs and the expected answers into one number you can compare across runs.

sections.title: How it works
sections.text: Choose the metric from the decision it supports. Ranking quality, classification accuracy and calibration answer different questions, and a model can lead on one and trail on another.

sections.title: Example
sections.text: A spam filter judged only on accuracy looks excellent when almost nothing is spam. Precision and recall show what accuracy hides.

items.title: Latency cheat sheet
items.summary: Round numbers worth having in your head. Illustrative values, not measurements.

sections.title: Quick facts
sections.text:
| Operation | Order of magnitude |
|---|---|
| Read from memory | nanoseconds |
| Read from a local disk | microseconds to milliseconds |
| Call a service in the same region | milliseconds |
| Call a service across regions | tens to hundreds of milliseconds |

- Tail latency is set by the slowest dependency.
- Fan-out multiplies the chance of hitting a slow one.

items.title: Quantization
items.summary: Store and compute with fewer bits to fit more model in less memory.

sections.title: Definition
sections.text: Quantization represents a model's weights, and sometimes its activations, with lower-precision numbers than the ones it was trained with.

sections.title: How it works
sections.text: Values are mapped onto a smaller set of levels with a scale and an offset. The mapping is chosen to lose as little accuracy as the task allows.

sections.title: Trade-offs
sections.text: CATALOG_PREMIUM_CANARY__DO_NOT_LEAK premium analysis of the accuracy and speed trade-off.

sections.title: Failure modes
sections.text: CATALOG_PREMIUM_CANARY__DO_NOT_LEAK premium catalogue of how quantization fails.

items.title: Retrieval-augmented generation
items.summary: Fetch relevant passages first, then let the model answer from them.

sections.title: Definition
sections.text: The system retrieves passages related to the question and places them in the prompt, so the model answers from supplied evidence rather than memory alone.

sections.title: When to use
sections.text: Use it when answers must reflect content that changes, or that the model was never trained on.

sections.title: Trade-offs
sections.text: You gain freshness and traceability. You add a retrieval step that can fail silently and a longer prompt to pay for.

items.title: Scaling laws
items.summary: How model quality tends to change as size, data and compute grow.

sections.title: Definition
sections.text: A scaling law is an empirical relationship between a model's quality and the resources spent training it.

sections.title: Why it matters
sections.text: It lets a team predict what a larger run would buy before paying for it, and decide how to split a fixed budget.

sections.title: Example
sections.text: Doubling data while holding model size fixed improves quality by a shrinking amount each time, which is the pattern a fitted curve captures.

items.title: Tokenization
items.summary: Splitting text into the pieces a model actually reads.

sections.title: Definition
sections.text: Tokenization breaks text into units, often word fragments, and maps each to an integer the model can consume.

items.title: Field notes
items.summary: A topic whose classification has not been published yet.

sections.title: Definition
sections.text: This item carries no category, so it appears in the full topic list and in none of the category groups.

sections.title: Field notes
sections.text: A section type this page does not know about is kept, in the order the API gave it, under deeper reference.

items.title: Vector index
items.summary: A structure that finds the stored points nearest to a query point quickly.

sections.title: Definition
sections.text: A vector index organises embeddings so that a nearest-neighbour query does not have to compare against every stored point.

sections.title: When to use
sections.text: Use one once the collection is too large to scan, and approximate answers are acceptable.

sections.title: Trade-offs
sections.text: Faster search costs memory and some recall. Tuning the index moves the balance between the two.
